messages.subject_clean: Need some If Then R code help
messages.body_plain:
Karl:  You provided me with some useful code (in boldface below) a while back for identifying the member of each high genotypic identity pair that has the least marker genotyping of the pair.  The code works well for wh objects that contain two or more pairs, but fails if there is only one (or no) pair.  Not knowing R that well, is there some simple R code that can be used to “jump over” (i.e., not execute) the code between the two italic cmds (my feeble attempts to date to develop that this IF THEN R code).  Any help will be appreciated as I am trying to automate the below code for repeated use in a batchfile for use with multiple populations.  - Jim

wh <- which(ALLpairs > 0.90, arr=TRUE)

wh

# Below cmds order pair members by their index nos - low (row) & high (col),

# so that ONLY a low - high index member arrangement shows for each pair.

wharrLH <- wh[wh[,1] < wh[,2],]

wharrLH

wh <- wh[wh[,1] < wh[,2],]

wh

# The below nt[wh] cmd outputs the number of marker genotypes for each of the

# indexed individuals in the population - zero genotypes for non-SG individuals.

nt <- ntyped(OBJNAME)

nt

# Let's repeat two cmds below to get clear info on the high identity pairs

wh

matrix(nt[wh],ncol=2)

# Below set of cmds moves the least genotyped F2 of each pair to the right

# col, so that this F2 member of the pair can be dropped from the population.

# Note:  Below cmd set works only if there are at least two rows in nrow(wh).

# I need an if then cmd set that would not execute the below cmd set IF

# only one row is present in the wh object (and also for zero rows)!

#a if (nrow(wh)<2) then skip below cmd set and go to #b below

todrop <- rep(NA, nrow(wh))

for(i in seq(along=todrop)) {

if(nt[1] <= nt[2]) todrop[i] <- wh[i,1]

else todrop[i] <- wh[i,2]

}

todrop    # Let's check on the contents of this todrop

#b if(nt[1] <= nt[2]) todrop <- wharrLH[[1]] else todrop <- wharrLH[[2]]

todrop    # Let's check on the contents of THIS todrop

# Now we will retain all individuals except those index #s in the todrop list

nind(OBJNAME)

OBJNAME <- subset(OBJNAME,ind=paste0("-",todrop))

nind(OBJNAME)

messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,
Thank you very much for describing in such a detail.
After I compared the scatterplots of phenotypes against genotypes of F2 and F3, I immediately understood what you meant.
It seemingly a couple of phenotypes showed F3 clusters, i.e. F3 phenotypic values are significantly different from the ones of F2, because of their high homozygosity and low phenotypic variances.
Although QTL in the other phenotypes are luckily supported by either QTL mapping with the F2 or the F3 dataset (We think we can safely say these are "real" QTL), I should keep in my mind above facts.
Anyway, Thank you very much for your comments. I really appreciate them!

Thank you.
All the best,
masato

On Friday, November 30, 2012 3:34:13 PM UTC-5, Karl Broman wrote:
> It's not so surprising that there would be significant peaks when you ignore relationships that would go away when you take account of relationships.
>
> The reason you need to use QTLRel and take account of the relationships is that those relationships among individuals results in non-independence.  A plot of phenotype vs genotype may appear to show a significant difference, but you can't easily account for the dependencies, in studying such a figure.
>
> I'm not sure how you will discriminate between your two hypotheses, but I would add that it is my understanding that the F3 individuals are actually less valuable, in terms of power to detect QTL, than that number of F2s, because of the non-independence.  The value of the F3s is mostly for mapping precision, due to the increased number of recombinants.
>
> But if the F3s are showing a high degree of homozygosity, or if they're showing little variation in the phenotype, then they won't be very helpful for mapping precision, either: you need variation both in the phenotype and in the genotypes if you wish to establish an association and so map QTL.
>
> karl
>
> On Nov 22, 2012, at 12:04 AM, Masato <yossy...@yahoo.co.jp> wrote:
>
> > Dear Karl and R/qtl discussion group members,
> > This can be novice question but I am shamelessly asking it since I couldn't find an answer after puzzling for a while.
> > I have performed QTL mapping for an animal (fish) behavior using F2 and F3 generations with r/qtl and QTLRel. To Karl, thank you very much for your kind helpful advice in the other day!
> > The combining F2 with F3 sounds unusual but our idea was to gain further phenotypic variance as well as higher resolution by extra recombination events in order to yield higher statistical power in the limited time. I, of course, had a problem of the relatedness among F2 and F3 so that I ran QTL mapping under QTLRel environment to resolve this.
> > Then another problem came up when I compared the results of scanOne between with and without relatedness (= variance component) to see how they were different. Surprisingly, a lot of significant QTL peaks (over p=0.05 permutation threshold) in the “without relatedness”-QTL scan were gone in the “with relatedness”-QTL scan, suggesting that many of QTL peaks in the “without relatedness”-scan were the false positives. This can be true but, when I take a look at the plotPXG at a couple of fake QTLs, the most of F3 (not F2) were BB homozygotes and they drag the phenotype to the one direction (such as, if the behavior ranges 0.0 – 1.0 and the average of F2 is 0.5, many of F3, which have BB genotype, show ~1.0).  This can raise two different hypotheses: (1) “B” allele has a genuine effect to drag the behavioral phenotype toward 1.0, or (2) most of F3 phenotypes are ~1.0 so that wherever the genomic loci have skewed genotype ratio (such as AA:AB:BB are 0%:10%:90% in F3, respectively), the “high (~1.0)” phenotype is always associated with BB genotype at such loci if F3 individual number is large enough against F2.
> > I imagine QTLRel is for resolving these two hypotheses but I would like to perform multiple QTL mapping to control noise-variance and its too hard to perform it under QTLRel to me (because I must handle a lot of command functions without making mistakes or misunderstandings).
> > I would really appreciate it if anyone suggests and/or advices me alternative methods to separate above two hypotheses.
> > I saw multiple skewed-genotype loci since I have developed F3 through the marker-assisted selection of F2 parents. high (~1.0)-behavior. I successfully got F3 with high (~1.0)-behavioral scores and expected the skewed genotype around the marker region in these F3 but, with some unknown reason, I saw the skewed genotype in totally unlinked LG too. This fact motivates me to separate above two hypotheses to recover “genuine” QTLs.
> >
> > I appreciate your time and kind thoughts in advance.
> > Thank you!
> >
> > Masato

Rqtl User Group & Karl:

I have a question about dealing with the outputted results of the calc.errorlod cmd in my multiple F2 populations (n=~250) for which the two phenotypic decile extremes were selectively genotyped (SG) with 450 to 500 markers in a genome of 2300 cM Kosambi (i.e., about 1 marker on average per 5 cM of distance).

The calc.errorlod cmd generates a large list of markers (see below example) in most of my F2 pops, primarily because the chromosome marker order and cM distances used in my *.csv file come from a published Ver. 4.0 (2010) marker map for soybean.  It has been acknowledged that this map (like all genetic maps) probably has some marker mis-order within tightly linked marker sets.  I surmise that such mis-order is probably reflected in the calc.errorlod cmd output as markers with repeated appearance (e.g.,  S30182, S14052).  I have too few genotyped individuals (50 in the decile SG’d 250 F2s) to construct a reliable intrinsic map for each F2, and the small F2 genotype numbers would likely have mis-order as well, not to mention unreliable marker distance estimates).  I will likely be some time before an updated Ver. 5.0 soybean genetic map is published.  In the meantime, I propose simply dropping  markers with multiple appearances in the below list (e.g., S30182, S14052), given that the removal of one tightly linked but mis-ordered marker would obviously still leave me with good markers in that close genomic region to use going forward.

What do you Rqtl users think about my proposal?

BTW, if I were to do this dropping of markers with n as the chosen number of repeat occurrences (e.g., say n = 4 or more), is there some simple R code I could use to put those markers into a todrop object?  The reason I ask for R help is that I would like to automate this process in a batchfile that I now use for error-checking in my multiple F2 populations.  Currently, I do it this kind of dropping manually and then use some code Karl provided to me earlier for “cleaning up” (i.e., change marker genotype to missing) the remaining markers in the below list (assumed – with some risk, of course- to be erroneous genotypings for a LOD score of 6 or more).

I will appreciate hearing your opinion on this subject and your R coding help if possible.  Unfortunately, my practical knowledge of R coding is very feeble, though I certainly love using Rqtl for its error-checking modules before one even THINKS about conducting a QTL analysis!

Jim

> I am building linkage maps using double haploid (DH) populations.
> 1) I used genotypes=c("A","B") as parameter of read.cross(). However, the data were treated as backcross population as shown in the logfile(--Cross type: bc). The write.cross() output gives AA and AB as well. Please could you tell me how to deal with DH population?

After loading your cross with read.cross, use class(mycross)[1] <- "dh"

  mycross <- read.cross("csv", "", "myfile.csv", genotypes=c("AA","BB"))
  class(mycross)[1] <- "dh"

The only real change in the analysis concerns the labeling of genotypes (as "AA"/"BB" rather than "AA"/"AB").

> 2) A warning message in summary.cross(): some chromosomes > 1000 cM in length; there may be a problem with the genetic map (Perhaps it is in basepairs?). Is there an explanation?

You can ignore this.  For QTL analysis, we need marker positions in cM.  In some cases, users give marker positions in basepairs; if one then uses calc.genoprob with step=1, this can cause problems with available memory (and computation time), as you'll be calculating QTL genotype probabilities millions of positions.

karl

messages.body_plain:
R/qtl doesn't currently include facilities to do interval mapping for segregation distortion.

I would look carefully at the genotype frequencies in both the long- and short-lived individuals at the markers where you see deviation from the expected frequencies in the long-lived individuals.  Is there real evidence for these markers being associated with longevity, or are the regions showing segregation distortion in all individuals?

karl

messages.body_plain:
Hi. I've been trying to analyze a binary trait with R/QTL, and find the odd result that running a simple Scanone (HK or EM) almost everything is "significant" by permutation tests (even just glancing at the chart, I have LOD scores >6 along almost the entire chromosomes, actually greater than 10 for most loci). Yet if I run qtlbim, I find actual peaks (based on LPD, which the authors suggest is akin to LOD scores, but in their bayesian framework). (Note I'm using the most recent package, R version 2.15 and qtl_1.26-14, and I don't think it's a coding error because I have since downloaded a dataset from a published paper and I can replicate their scanone LOD plots in R/qtl.) I would in this case think that the regular "qtl" package is preferable to "qtlbim" because the latter will not allow analysis of the X chromosome, but is there any suggestion for what could cause inflated LOD scores across the entire chromosome and so differentiate R/qtl from qtlbim? I'm fine with trying most any package (preference for free ones of course), but while we have some issues with the X chromosome that we need to work out, we think the X chromosome is important and so we do want the option of analyzing data from it.

I'll note I am using the MSG software (Andolfatto and Stern's work) to read in conditional probabilities directly, but I think I finally got this to work -- esp as I can replicate the results from one of their published plots.

If someone has time, any suggestions are greatly appreciated, because I'm a bit baffled on how to proceed or what's causing the huge qtl/qtlbim discrepancy.
